title: Over 400 Indian-Origin Scholars in 27 Countries Warn Against 'Anarchy' Over Election Protests
excerpt: Students, researchers and alumni affiliated with MIT, Oxford, Harvard and other universities signed a joint statement, 'Spare India from Anarchy,' condemning protests against the Election Commission and urging disputes be settled inside constitutional institutions.
body:
• More than 400 Indian-origin students, researchers and alumni from universities in 27 countries have signed a joint statement titled "Spare India from Anarchy," condemning protests against the Election Commission of India.
  • The signatories, affiliated with institutions including MIT, Oxford, Cambridge, Harvard, Stanford and the London School of Economics, say street protests are being used to sow doubt about India's democratic and constitutional institutions.
  • The statement invokes B. R. Ambedkar's call to "hold fast to constitutional methods" and urges political forces to resolve differences through debate and dialogue inside constitutional institutions.
  • For Indian students and researchers abroad, the statement is a reminder that disputes at home over the Election Commission and electoral rolls are now being contested publicly by the diaspora itself, on campuses across four continents.

More than 400 Indian-origin students, researchers and alumni from universities across 27 countries have issued a joint statement condemning opposition protests against the Election Commission of India, describing them as an attempt to undermine public confidence in constitutional institutions and delegitimise democratic processes, according to Careers360.

The statement, titled "Spare India from Anarchy," criticised the use of what the signatories called anarchic street protests to challenge democratic processes and warned against subverting constitutional democracy in the name of defending it.

What the statement says

The signatories argued that a plan had been hatched to sow doubt about Indian democracy by weaponising matters that are pending before the courts and amplifying them on the streets. "An unconscionable and devious plan of sowing seeds of doubt in Indian democracy has been hatched by weaponising sub judice matters, which is then amplified on the streets by leaning on anarchist forces, which have historically and philosophically never believed in constitutional form of governance. All in the name of saving democracy," the statement said.

"In the seven decades since independence, Indian democracy has proved its resilience repeatedly. Institutions have flourished, checks and balances have functioned admirably, and peaceful transition of power has remained an enduring hallmark."

— "Spare India from Anarchy" joint statement

The statement lamented what it called a frenzy of election denial, relentless questioning of constitutional institutions and a preference for "street over Sansad" — Parliament — in certain quarters. Unfavourable election outcomes had led to questions about procedural integrity, adverse judgements had provoked commentary on judicial independence, and even the Armed Forces, described as the country's most apolitical institution, had been drawn into partisan discourse, the signatories said.

Who signed, and from where

The signatories are based in, or have studied in, 27 countries across four continents, including the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Ireland, Italy, Spain, Sweden, Norway, Poland, Ukraine, Russia, South Korea, Japan, Singapore, Malaysia, Israel, the United Arab Emirates, Kazakhstan, Georgia and the Philippines, according to reporting on the statement. Their affiliations include the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the universities of Oxford and Cambridge, Princeton, Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Columbia, the London School of Economics, the National University of Singapore, Seoul National University, the University of Manchester and the University of Toronto. The statement clarified that the affiliations do not imply endorsement by those universities.

"We remain amazed at the irony of all. But more importantly, as informed people who have stakes in the future of this country and travel the world identifying as 'Indians,' we are deeply anguished at this state of affairs," the signatories said.

The dispute behind the protests

The statement comes amid protests by opposition parties against the Election Commission, with opposition leaders questioning the integrity of electoral processes and raising allegations of irregularities in elections. The signatories acknowledged that dissent is an essential ingredient of democracy, but said they refused to remain silent spectators to what they described as the subversion of the democratic apparatus in its guise.

Invoking B. R. Ambedkar, the architect of the Constitution, the statement recalled his warning to hold fast to constitutional methods and abandon the "grammar of anarchy." It urged social and political forces to resolve differences through debate, discussion, dialogue and dissent under the roof of constitutional institutions, and expressed solidarity with democratic forces globally.

Why it matters beyond India

Joint statements of this kind have become a recurring feature of diaspora politics, with Indian students and academics abroad organising publicly on contested questions at home. This intervention is notable for its scale — more than 400 signatories — and for the breadth of its institutional affiliations, spanning universities in North America, Europe, Asia and Australia. For the signatories, the argument is that the credibility of India's institutions shapes how Indians abroad are seen and how much weight their own democratic participation carries in the countries where they study and work.

There has been no indication in the reporting of a formal response from the Election Commission or opposition parties to this specific statement. The underlying dispute remains before political and legal forums in India, and further diaspora statements on both sides are likely.
